nodes.text: XIII. ON THE SINGLE LIFE OF CLERICS.

Some time ago, dearest sons, I had indeed promised you a letter which, commending the rules of all conduct from the law, would contain in summary everything that applies generally to all clerics for directing the rule of discipline. But because some among you have now publicly fallen into disgrace through living with women, I have been compelled by the Lord's rebuke to write to you specifically on this matter also. On account of your negligence He commanded wretched me to give, with fitting severity, the order that clerics should not live with women. And although this admonition would be sufficient on the authority of my letter alone, nevertheless, so that no one may mock me as a dreamer, as his brothers mocked Joseph, we add the firm support of the Scriptures, so that all may know that the Lord commands by revelation in this way too what He is known from the written word to have commanded before; and that we are not adulterating the word of the Lord, or wishing to boast vainly of revelations, but that in reporting thus before the sight of the Lord we do not lie in what we say. Just so we trust that we have heard no lie from the Lord, taking for ourselves the words of the apostle Paul, who declares: "For we are not," he says, "like many, adulterating the word of God, but out of sincerity, as from God, before Him, we speak in Christ." Placed, therefore, in the greatest grief over certain wasted members of our body, and groaning at the loss suffered by the lamenting Church, which through our sluggishness is reduced day by day to excessive fewness, we believe we are relieved in some measure by this: that the negligence of certain people cannot harm our diligence, since our letters have never failed them, letters which have made up to everyone for my absence by their frequency. Let each one who scorns [them] write himself down as guilty of his own disregard; but we, with a free countenance, cry out to the scorners what Solomon reproaches with confidence: "Since I called," he says, "and you did not obey, and I stretched out my words, and you did not attend, but made my counsels void, and did not attend to my rebukes, therefore I too will laugh at your ruin. I will rejoice over you when destruction comes upon you, when sudden tumult comes upon you, and overthrow like a storm, and when distress and assault come upon you. For it will be that when you call on me, I will not hear you. The wicked will seek me and will not find [me]; for they hated wisdom. And they did not take up the word of the Lord, nor were they willing to attend to my counsels. For they despised my reproofs; and therefore they will eat the fruits of their own way and will be filled with their own impiety."

Now our exhortation turns to you, whom we do not want to experience such headlong falls into ruin. Fear as much as you can the destruction of such a fall, and in this overthrow of those who are slipping let their examples terrify us. Too headlong is he who strives to cross over when he has seen another fall, and very unbridled is he in whom no fear is struck when another perishes. But he is a lover of his own safety who avoids running into another's death. And he is prudent who becomes anxious at the disasters of others, as Solomon confirms, saying: "The shrewd man, seeing evil punished, will be greatly instructed"; and again: "When the impious fall, the just will be greatly terrified." Confidence that entrusts its life to dangers as though they were certain is a foe, and slippery is the hope that hopes to be saved amid the kindlings of sin. Victory is uncertain when fighting amid hostile weapons, and deliverance is impossible for one surrounded by flames not to burn. Solomon denies this, saying: "Who will bind fire in his bosom and not burn his garments? Or who will walk upon coals of fire and not burn his feet? So he who goes in to his neighbour's wife will not be unharmed, nor anyone who touches her." Believe, I beg you, believe divine faithfulness rather than your own: for whatever it promises cannot deceive, as the Lord says: "It is easier," He says, "for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke to fall from the law." And again: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." It is we, then, who deceive ourselves whenever we believe in a disordered way, supposing that the precepts of the law can be changed by our faith, so that we hope that chastity may be kept unshaken while men and women mingle freely.

Hardly will anyone drink poison and live. One who sleeps on a riverbank must fear that he may fall, since the apostle says: "Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." In this matter it is better to fear well than to trust badly. And it is more useful for a man to recognise that he is weak so that he may prove strong, than to wish to seem strong and turn out weak. On this matter the apostle rebukes the presumptuous, saying: "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself." Certainly a self-deceiver beguiles his own soul when, not guarding against them, he commits himself to things that are harmful. But he takes safer counsel for himself who, always distrustful around evil things, dreads every harmful appearance. Solomon set out the difference between these, saying: "The wise man, by fearing, will turn aside from all evil; but the fool, trusting in himself, mingles with the wicked." A great counsel of divine wisdom has been found, whereby we are freed by the help of fear. Great are the economies of providence, that at times virtue and victory come about through fear. Great remedies has the Lord bestowed for salvation, so that even the fearful man may have praise, as Solomon repeats, saying: "Blessed is the man who reveres all things through fear." Inestimable is the Lord's mercy, which has bestowed glory on His man from every side, and incomprehensible His kindness, which has given prizes according to the battles, so that by confidence we may overcome the savagery of men and by fear conquer the allurements of women, provided that the Lord works glories over us both from strength and from weakness, so that in all things and through all things He may show Himself almighty, distributing different kinds of triumph, so that wars may be won by us as much by counsel as by strength; nor, if we were to conquer by the strength of faith alone, would the works of wisdom be made void against Solomon. Now, therefore, the arms of wisdom must be borne, where the female and the male sex declare battle. Hence Solomon instructs thus, saying: "Make prudence known to you," he says, "so that it may keep you from the strange and most evil woman." See now that in this war it is prudence, not faith, that has been given us as victor, prudence which would free us by the remedy of fearfulness; and consider what arms are now to be taken up, if you wish to have the help of the law. Be fearful, so that you may be fearless; and although fear in a contest seems to be weakness, yet according to the word of the apostle, strength is made perfect in weakness. Separate yourselves, I beseech you, separate yourselves from this pestilent contagion.

The farther each one is from adversities, the less he feels adversities. He is less goaded by pleasures who is not where pleasures abound. And he suffers less from the troubles of avarice who does not see riches, if we accept the apostle's assurance: "Those who wish," he says, "to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a man into perdition and destruction." Not otherwise is he exposed to temptations who is joined to a woman, in whom there is nothing else but what wounds the one who comes near. The female form has become the sting of sin, and the condition of death arose from nowhere else than from the substance of woman. Solomon recalls this for our vigilance, saying: "From a woman came the beginning of sin, and because of her we all die." From that we are held mortal, and yet we do not fear. What if we were already immortal? Through a woman Christ has indeed set us free, but we ought to dread that from which we still die. Deliverance itself will be established in the woman then, when the death which had come through a woman is conquered in turn by us. But if stumbling blocks still hold sway around us through a woman, we have certainly squandered the deliverance of Christ: for this hope of freedom, which we believe Christ has bestowed on our faith, remains for the future, when a woman will not harm us at all, once death itself has been made void. For if we think that we are now beyond the temptation of a woman's darts, then nothing remains for the heavenly kingdom. Not undeservedly does the apostle rebuke such notions, saying: "Already you are sated, already you have become rich; without us you reign; and would that you did reign!" So the time of struggle is still being waged, and death still rages through woman even now. I lie if we do not see from this the destruction of very many. How many bishops, and of what standing, and clerics together with laymen, after trampling down the contests of confession and victory, after mighty works and signs and wonders shown everywhere, are known to have suffered shipwreck along with all these, when they choose to sail in a fragile ship? How many lions has one delicate weakness tamed, which, though it is cheap and wretched, makes prey of the great? Solomon speaks of this, saying: "The price of a harlot is as much as one loaf, but a woman captures precious souls."

These things are treated before our eyes, and we are restrained by no terrors: what would we do if we heard of histories as matters only of report? But this is always the unbelief of human hardness, that not only by hearing but even by seeing it does not believe that others have perished, unless it sees itself perishing too; nor is it shaken by the deaths of its companions, as long as it supposes they deserved it or were weak. But it confidently thinks that it itself deserves much or is very strong, not knowing that examples are offered to all when punishments have been inflicted on some, as the Lord sets forth in the Gospel and says: "Do you think that these Galileans who suffered such things were sinners above all the Galileans? No, I tell you: unless you repent, you will perish likewise, as those on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them. Do you think that they too were debtors above all the people living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you: if you do not repent, you will perish likewise."

We wonder that Adam was led astray through Eve, though no examples of the dying had gone before him, only a single command had bound him, while now neither countless deaths nor endless commands restrain us. To us it is fittingly said, after the Lord's rebuke: "If Adam had seen the deaths that have taken place among you, he would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable for Adam on the day of judgement than for you." Far, very far away let this plague be, this pestilence and hidden ruin. O how disordered is nearness to a woman! It shoots its darts, and the brigandage of sins is its neighbour. In this companionship there is no sincerity worth approving, for it holds clashes as if from turbulent waves. In this familiarity friendly concord does not dwell, since it creates nothing but discordant enmities. The Lord did indeed make woman a helper for man, but through the serpent's envy she took on the role of an enemy. And if she who was born from her own husband tempts even to this day the very man to whom she is joined, how much more she who is coupled to a man though joined by no law? And if those who are two grown together in one flesh prick one another with mutual temptations, what do those do who were neither born nor joined in one flesh? Especially since he who is drawn away by love of another is no longer allowed to call upon God, nor is he permitted to think on divine things who has sought for himself someone to whom he may show household care. For this reason the apostle advises thus, saying: "I want you to be without anxiety. He who is without a wife is anxious how he may please God; but he who has a wife thinks of the things of this world, how he may please his wife." What is there now to delight in this union, in which there are only battles? Or what benefit commends it, where there are no conjugal duties, since even these cannot be free from danger? Everything that belongs to a woman is an occasion of falling, and union with her is always hostile. By her compact she causes great troubles, and on the man to whom she has unlawfully attached herself she inflicts an incurable wound. Sparks leap from coals, rust is bred from iron, asps hiss out diseases, and a woman pours forth the pestilence of lust, which Solomon compares thus, saying: "From garments comes the moth, and from a woman the iniquity of a man."
I want to know what this shared affection is, what this discord of disease.

always wavering, he throws his own resolve into confusion, attacking it with tottering counsels. Why has he taken a woman to himself who scorned to marry a wife? Why does everyone who does not eat meat fill his dwelling with preparations of meat? And why does he who does not drink wine enjoy the delight of wine? As if the mind were not often fed by an abundance of foods merely by having them, without tasting, and the mind more often roused by the mere fragrance of scented wine. Why does he wish through hypocrisy to be called abstinent by men, and in secret to be swollen with meat and drunkenness? Many have riches which they deny to their own use but keep out of greed; if no greed had clung to them, they would not possess the emblems of greed either. But because they are possessed by greed, they enjoy in mind what they do not touch in use. So he who has despised the bond of marriage is bound in another way by a woman's bonds: though he is joined in no intercourse, he is still always delighted by desire, by sight, by conversation, by companionship. For if he had no desire for a woman, he would never take a woman for his delights. Indeed, moreover, he has given me a suspect resolve, who took an unlawful woman and refused a lawful one: unless I am mistaken, he contrived in public to promise holiness to men and in secret not to be without a wife. Two devices, of lust and of holiness, on this side and that, are to be marvelled at, which each cover the other and each betray the other. This ingenious eunuch and adulterer cheats himself while he takes counsel for himself, and while he seeks both. He has achieved neither, so that he is hardly to be reckoned holy who does not enjoy a true union, since the apostle Paul says: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife." But I grant that the chastity of this continence has not been violated; yet he offers a bad reputation to the suspicious, and in vain guards within, with toilsome struggle, the good of chastity, which he causes to be defamed without, destroying the teaching of the apostle Paul, who both foresees and warns: "Why," he says, "is my freedom judged by an unbelieving conscience? If I partake with thanks, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?" It is worse than adultery to lead a criminal continence and to make holiness infamous. He brings blasphemy on the religion he has practised who does not fulfil before all what he professes, lest Christianity be believed a deceit and adultery seem clothed in the veil of holiness. For this reason the Lord forewarns thus in the Gospel, saying: "So let your light shine before men, that seeing your good works they may magnify your Father who is in heaven." The apostle Paul follows this too, saying: "Therefore let your good not be blasphemed." And again: "Providing things that are good not only before God but also before men." And in another place: "So whether you eat or drink or do anything, do all things to the glory of God, and be without stumbling block to Jews and Greeks and to the church of God, just as I too please all men in all things."

But perhaps it is objected: what of his saying, in turn, "If I wished to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ"? The sayings of the law never exclude one another, but all their answers are fixed to definite places. There it is not permitted to please men, where the will of men does not take in the will of the Lord; but where men accept what advances the glory of God, the apostle Paul himself commanded that it be made known to all. "Let each of us," he says, "please his neighbour for good edification." How far, then, can he expect the reward of holiness who not only provokes blasphemy of holiness from unbelievers, but also offers a ruinous example to the faithful? So that the weak, under the pretext of love, commit fornication subtly, and the chaste man most unchastely gives instruction in chastity, destroying what the apostle Paul threatens: "Has the weak brother perished," he says, "through your knowledge, for whom Christ suffered? Thus, sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ." And indeed it is fitting not only for the young but also for the old to take thought for the weakness of the brothers, lest old age provoke youth to perish, old age from which all salutary teachings ought to proceed; as Eleazar in the book of the Maccabees declares and says: "[I would rather] be sent ahead into the underworld [than desert the laws of my fathers]. For it is not worthy of our age to pretend, so that many of the young, thinking that Eleazar at ninety years old had gone over to the life of foreigners, should themselves, because of my pretence and for a short and corruptible span of life, be led astray through me, and I should bring hatred and stain upon my old age." He preferred to throw his life to torments rather than become anyone's teacher of perdition; and we, where there are no torments, are unwilling to put the brothers who are to be saved before mere passing pleasures, and are not content to benefit ourselves as much as others without any tortures, whereas he did not wish to live when he was about to die, as he went on below, saying: "Therefore, departing life bravely, I shall appear worthy of my old age, and I shall leave to the young a brave example, that with ready spirit and bravely they may depart by an honourable death for the weighty and holy laws." Since this befits even laymen, so as not to set before outsiders occasions for blasphemy or before the brotherhood an opportunity for fornication, then above all this necessity binds clerics vehemently, on whom either religion blasphemed or the brotherhood lost will inflict a double penalty. Nor will those who have supplied fuel for sin to foreigners and brothers find any comfort at all in the Lord's judgement. For this reason the apostle Paul instructs Titus thus, saying: "Showing yourself an example of good deeds, in teaching, in integrity, in gravity, in sound and irreproachable speech, so that the adversary may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say of us." And again: "Show good faith to all," he says, "so that they may display the good teaching of our Lord the Saviour in all things." So too he writes to Timothy, saying: "Be a pattern to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in chastity." The apostle Peter also satisfies this, saying: "Let your conduct among the gentiles be good," he says, "so that, in that in which they disparage us as evildoers, they may glorify the Lord from your good works." And again: "For so," he says, "is the will of God, that by doing good you may silence the ignorance of foolish men."

Nor let anyone set before himself and say: "I want to have something to conquer." For that is to say: "I desire to live under ruin." Who is so foolish as to wish to be pressed into toil when he is offered a gentler way to triumph? For it is not a double triumph to be proved victor in the presence of a woman, rather than in solitude to keep the pledge of holiness whole. And since the title of glory is one, in this case the strong man who toils a great deal is futile, and is rewarded equally with him who has conquered with little toil. What of the fact that he, on the contrary, is counted perfect who shows himself cut off in every part from feelings for women? For the Lord in the Gospel calls him perfect who has cut off his whole patrimony from his own use. Surely even for anyone alone, daily triumphs for chastity are not lacking, since the human body never ceases to assail the spirit with carnal desires, which the apostle affirms, saying: "The flesh," he says, "lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish." You now have your own flesh to overcome always: why do you want to bring in another as well? No one wishes to add a worse fever on top of one fever, lest he begin to suffer from an incurable semi-tertian fever, which no physician could relieve. Nor does anyone take up another's burden on top of his own, lest, weighed down by two burdens, he be sunk down to the underworld. Hence the prophet Jeremiah teaches thus that the weight of holiness must be borne alone: "It is good," he says, "for a man when he has borne a heavy yoke in his youth: he will sit alone and be silent, since he has taken a heavy yoke upon himself."

But some malicious follower may take refuge in the saying of the apostle Paul, saying: "Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ." These are not the burdens that the apostle Paul commands to be carried; rather, [he commands] that, bearing with one another, no discord should divide us, and that we should give mutual help to brothers placed in temptations; not that we should procure temptations for ourselves through women, but rather that we should lighten the weights of temptations, since he knows what the yoke of holiness is like, that it is scarcely borne [even] alone. Concerning this not only he himself but also the Lord was unwilling to lay down a fixed precept, saying: "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given." And again: "He who can receive [it], let him receive [it]." If, then, the greatness of this weight is borne with difficulty alone, how will it be borne if it is made heavier by doubled weights? And if almost all who are alone scarcely manage to withstand the snares of the flesh, what are those doing who do not hesitate to throw themselves on swords hanging over them from either side? I say more. If husbands and wives, who carry out their conjugal desires daily, are not sufficient for one another, what are those to do who join themselves to women to increase the assaults? A woman's appearance, meeting [a man] unexpectedly or in passing for an hour, shoots arrows, as it were, into another's eyes. When simple reverence is not free, what goes on there where a woman takes on the boldness of freedom in sharing a dwelling? When, in household tasks, she now bares her arms and thighs at her wool-working, now, being hot, uncovers her limbs, now, tired, tosses about, or at times dissolves in laughter, now shows endearments, and, what is more poisonous than all, delights to sing psalms or songs? It is more bearable to hear a basilisk hissing than her singing. Against her Solomon makes us cautious thus, saying: "Do not be constantly with a dancing-girl, nor listen to her, lest perhaps you perish by her power." I pass over the rest, which are more to be ashamed of than spoken; I say only this: to see a woman broken down in grief or in anger is already not without allurement. What do we say if you see her merry, or, what is worse, coaxing? Let me say it once for all: every unfitting companionship with women is the glue of sins and the poisoned birdlime with which the devil goes fowling. Unsuitable is the society of women, whose companionship Solomon again teaches us to guard against in every way thus: "With another man's wife," he says, "do not sit at all, and do not wrangle with her over wine, lest perhaps your heart incline towards her and with your blood you slip into perdition."

Finally, if we trust that our mind will always persevere in this shared life, at least this ought to be suspect to us: lest the women themselves who live together with us be perhaps moved towards us, or be goaded by maddening incitements towards other loves on account of their impetuous age; and there will be a cause for us, what is worse, that without cause another's fornication stains us, with whom the occasion of a brothel is suggested to others, and we shall be swallowed up by the charge of another's guilt, for whose impurity we ourselves furnish the procuring. For this reason the apostle Paul instructs us concerning such things thus, saying: "If your brother is scandalised because of food, you no longer walk in love. Do not by your food destroy him for whom Christ died." And again: "It is good not to eat meat nor to drink wine, nor [anything] by which your brother stumbles or is scandalised or is weakened." And in another place: "Judge this rather," he says, "that you not put an obstacle or stumbling block before a brother." And of himself he says thus: "For this reason, if food scandalises my brother, I will not eat meat for ever, lest I scandalise my brother." Since, then, the detestable trouble of this cohabitation assails us, even if it cannot make adulterers, it nevertheless makes [us] procurers for adulterers and the incestuous. For who, as searcher of another's heart, would weigh the character of each one, and would presume to be a fighter against Satan on behalf of another person, and a fit guarantor before God? He is mad who promises anything about himself, not to say if he also seems to give a pledge for a woman, since the apostle Paul declares thus about himself, saying: "Not that I have already received, or am already justified, or am already perfect; but I follow on, if I may lay hold [of that] for which I too was laid hold of by Christ. Brothers, I do not reckon that I have yet laid hold; but one thing [I do]: forgetting what is behind, reaching towards what is ahead, I follow by the rule towards the palm of the heavenly calling of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let as many of us, then, as are perfect think this." And again: "To me," he says, "it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but neither do I judge myself. He who judges me is the Lord." And in another place: "Blessed," he says, "is he who does not judge himself in that by which he tests another." Although, then, we have nothing certain even about our own steadfastness, we who are shaken without ceasing among the waves of the world, enduring stormy onsets, yet if anyone has such great confidence in the immovability of his own firmness, let him at least anxiously dread lest he himself be a stumbling block to the eyes of others, and let him be terrified by the voice of the Lord threatening: "Woe," he says, "to this world because of stumbling blocks; but woe to that man through whom the stumbling block comes." If we fear and revere these threats of the Lord with a religious heart, let us dread our danger more from others than from ourselves, we who are bound by the apostle Paul to mutual benefits: "Each one," he says, "thinking not of what is his own, but of what is others'." And again: "Let no one seek what is his own, but what is another's."

But someone, seizing from Paul himself something to object, [says]: "Each one of us," he says, "will render account for himself to God, and each one will carry his own pack." He, then, who does not wish to render account for another ought not to take part, as an unlawful partner, in his affairs or business; and he who tries to be free or exempt in regard to others' packs should, on the opposite condition, keep nothing belonging to another in his charge. For he who has handled another's business must necessarily be subject to the other's account. He must be bound over for the loss or damage of the packs in whose house, under unsafe custody, a brother's packs have perished, since whatever in our house has been under less than adequate guard, or thieves have broken into, is ours, and whatever has been badly entrusted through our negligence is required of us. Only then are we free of one another, if nothing of another's property is kept with us.

Perhaps someone may say: "Then must we not even gather together at the house of prayer, lest someone scandalise someone?" This slanderous objection belongs to a heretical profession, which pleads from good things in order to assert evil ones, and prejudges holiness in order subtly to introduce impurity, and makes slanders out of what is lawful in order to be able to obtain what is unlawful. For this reason the apostle Paul pleads in advance against this heresy, saying: "Nevertheless neither is woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord." Far be it, far be it, that women should be barred everywhere or that permission should be granted everywhere. They have their places with a husband, with sons, with brothers, with parents, with slaves, and in the house of prayer only, alongside all the clerics. But in a single dwelling, without kinship, they do not fittingly have companions. This is the balance that stands level. But whatever has tilted the balance cannot stand, as Scripture says: "You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left," and the Lord in the Gospel: "What is more than this is from evil." Learn now the measure of moderation, you who through licence seek excess. Love women at the sacred solemnities and hate them in private association, if you wish to hold to the teaching of Solomon: "A time," he says, "for loving and a time for hating."

So the company of women is to be guarded against at the time when constant attendance on fleshly cares is carried on with continual unanimity, since amid its cares the flesh always stirs up the incitements of desire, and brings forth the kindlings of sin there where, handling its own advantages, it has felt itself relaxed a little by the thoughts of temporal life, as Solomon asserts, saying: "Earthly thought weighs down the mind that thinks many things." But in the gathering of the sacred rites, where the spirit is master, the handmaid, recognising herself, loses the use of her pleasure, and loses her wantonness too while heavenly things are treated, while the holy mysteries are celebrated: the whole of human nature is occupied, where all things are not human but divine; where veneration, or terror and trembling, is struck into all minds, the fleshly substance is surely buried. Even amid the very business of the flesh many neglect bodily pleasure, when the legions practise the exercises of arms, or the forum rings with lawsuits, or the lecture halls resound with letters, or merchants apply themselves urgently to trade, or craftsmen are bent on their crafts themselves: how much more where the work being done is not the fleshly work of men but the spiritual work of angels? Assaults can do nothing there where even the demons themselves give way, and no difference of either sex is allowed to be considered, where neither age nor rank but equality alone reigns; and, to speak more fully, all receive there such a disposition that even married life is unknown, where Christ speaks, is heard, is attended to, and through all things and in all things he alone is everything, as the apostle testifies, saying: "Where there is not," he says, "Jew and Greek, circumcision and foreskin, barbarian and Scythian, male and female, slave and free, but Christ [is] all things and in all things." This gathering it is plainly a glory to celebrate with women, in which there is no distinction of kind, to which it is permitted so far to make all equal without any difference that not even in baptism itself does anyone's nakedness blush, where the infancy of Adam and Eve is renewed, and [one] does not put off but rather receives a tunic.

But if even there there should be someone worse than the devil who is struck by the sight of women, our congregation is nevertheless blamed for no one, since it is gathered for heavenly things, not for earthly ones. Let him see to it who is there shameless with lustful gazes; he in no way harms another who has come forward not to a human being but to Christ for salvation. Indeed I will even shut out the objectors by their own objections, so that they yield not to my propositions but to their own. If at the sacred festivals the common assembly can be made to stumble, where the tempter, the devil himself, trembles, who promises himself to be steadfast there where the tempter boldly comes to meet him? And if we are in danger there where God's precepts gather us together, what are we doing where God's commands separate us? And if we are troubled there where we are fortified by the will of God, how much more where we have against us not only the devil but also the Lord? For with the sacrosanct commands divine protection is supplied to us, as Isaiah says: "He gave the law," he says, "as a help"; but without the divine commands there can be no defence.

It is one thing to do what God commands and another to resist his will. His commandments are to be kept in such a way that, if he commands something that seems unjust by human standards, it is believed just and is done, and if he commands what is just, it is reckoned just and is done; since what he commands cannot be without victory, he who is able, by justifying, to call injustice justice, and, by condemning, to prove justice a perverse injustice, whose will is the sole and true justice. For if everything whatever we do, we do only for this, that we may please the Lord, then surely that alone will be just which God, whom we long to please, has willed and commanded and approved. For since slaves cannot know of themselves what pleases their masters unless they follow their masters' orders, and since human beings themselves cannot recognise the wills of humans like themselves unless they have received what to observe, much more do mortals not know how to grasp the justice of the immortal God, unless he himself deigns to show the signs of his justices, as Solomon confirms, saying: "For which of men will be able to know the counsel of God? Or who will be able to think what God wills? The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our forethought uncertain. For the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things. We hardly estimate what is on earth, and what is before our eyes we find with labour; but what is in the heavens, who will search out? And who knows your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your holy spirit from the highest? And so the paths of those who are on earth were corrected, and men learned what pleases you, and were healed through wisdom." Those walking in darkness cannot show a light to themselves, unless the light offers itself of its own accord to those who do not see. So human blindness does not direct its way to God unless he himself shows the lamp of the law. Hence David speaks thus, saying: "Your word," he says, "is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." And again: "The precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes." This therefore is light-bringing, whatever has been made known by God; and this is worthy of God, which God himself declares acceptable to his will, so that he may exercise dominion through all things. Otherwise we would not be enrolled as slaves, nor would he himself be held as Lord, if we were allowed to render service according to our own will and chose the exercises of justice by our own judgement, not God's. Such people the apostle Paul brings to nothing, saying: "Ignorant," he says, "of God's justice and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to the justice of God." Let these so empty evasions and idly slanderous complaints now be removed from our midst. With God's help we do not fear to be united with women for spiritual acts, since we believe we are working justice by God's command, from which we know that defences are set under us. But in private, lodgings must be kept as separate as possible for continent clerics and virgins, because what God judges wicked cannot be just. Yet sharing a dwelling, even if no shameful practice is known in that sharing, inflames, because it is impossible for integrity to reach victory when it strives to fight against God's commands. For as much as the law supplies help to the obedient, so much does it stir up, indeed, sin in the disobedient, as the apostle says: "The power," he says, "of sin is the law." He, then, who commanded us to triumph with women in his sacred rites himself commands us to beware in private of battles with women.

There are indeed other necessities which compel us to see women in private as well, but these too the efficacy of divine precept or work enjoins: that we visit, that we offer comfort, that we wholesomely impart life-giving exhortations. Yet even in these duties no less care must be taken for our conduct, so that signs of purity may shine out in our activity. Let there be no lack of severity which can hold a woman in check under a cleric, so that she receives our very consolation with trembling and so perceives the affection of the visit that she reveres the cleric. And, not to be slow in ranging over every detail, everything whatever we do can be honourable if signs of honour always shine out in us, as the apostle Paul embraced all things, saying: "Let all your things be done honourably." And again: "As we instructed you," he says, "walk honourably." Whatever is done haphazardly does not turn out well, and what is done as holy is not holy unless what is holy is carried out in a holy manner, as Solomon asserts, saying: "For those who keep just things justly will be justified." Sincerity itself, therefore, must be kept sincerely, and all that belongs to the vow must also be marked in act, lest vows commend one thing and acts suggest another. On every side both the resolve of the will must be proved, and on every side the course of each contest must be completed, lest something be lacking for the triumph if the fight is not fought to the full. Hence the apostle Paul brings in lessons from contests: "But he too who strives in a contest," he says, "will not be crowned unless he has striven lawfully." And again: "Do you not know," he says, "that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. And everyone who strives in a contest is continent in all things; and they indeed to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible." This, then, is the fullness of holiness and the perfect palm: to have with oneself, on every side, nothing that one rejects, lest by keeping what one professes to hate one seem to love it.

But if someone says, "I hold my adversary captive, so that I may always mock him," let him see to it that the captive does not perhaps begin to prevail against him. A thief is never safely kept shut in with treasure, nor is a lamb safe living in one cage with a wolf. He has willed himself to be penetrated who has led his own enemy inside his gates, and he has set an internal sword under himself who has opened the place of his dwelling to the adversary's entry; and he who is confident in living with a stumbling block says to no purpose, "I want to be at peace with the devil," against the apostle, who says: "Do not give place to the devil." In every way, therefore, the place must be fortified where treasure is hidden, lest through a single hole the thief dig through the whole wall. For if, when attacking from outside, he is barely driven back by the walls, how strong will he be if he has received a dwelling within the walls? And if those who shut [the gates] against him are sometimes captured by him, how much more he who of his own accord has opened the entry to him, since Solomon says: "If the just man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the impious appear?" All cracks, then, not to speak of gates, must be closed, lest through one opening the whole camp be penetrated, and all the defences must be put in order, lest through a small unfortified part the whole city fall, as Solomon repeats, saying: "He who scorns small things will fall little by little."

But I am astounded at the judgement of this perversity, that a woman rather than a man is chosen by clerics for a shared life. Is a woman really as much more useful for a cleric's convenience as a continent man, or a boy, is of benefit to a continent man? Or will that be a seemly usefulness which an unseemly shared life produces? And where will be what Solomon says: "Every animal loves its like"? And again: "Birds gather to their like." But even if a woman were thought more useful, one ought not to put fleshly gains before the benefits of spiritual advantages, and it was better to put up with any useless man for the sake of protecting one's reputation than the good services of a woman with the most shameful reputation. Solomon compares this, saying: "Better," he says, "is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good." The devil's favours, then, are always contrived: exercising by them the ingenuity of his cunning, he helps those devoted to holiness with deceitful conveniences in order to destroy them; and supplying among the continent, as if necessary benefits, mutual assistances, he first drives man and woman to [live] together, so that, after he has made them inseparable through mutual comforts, he may kill those who give simple minds to keeping the vows of chastity; and, withdrawing for a while the weapons of his attack, as if a gentle patron he suggests proofs of holiness, until he has long nourished a hostile friendship between the two. He makes them affable to one another and serviceable, and, a hostile flatterer, removing all obstacles, he rejoices to lend effectiveness to their conveniences, so that, commending them to each other by every necessity, he may make them depend on one another in their accustomed consolation. He does not wish to hinder them in anything, lest he separate them spiritually as well as carnally. He makes them live unshaken, lest at an untimely moment the beginnings of their companionship disturb the compacts they have begun. To such an extent, while all look on, does he invite, foster and raise them up to the perfection of holiness that they reckon as God's favours the very adversities by which they are led to perish, not knowing that God never helps what he forbids. Flattering them, the devil prepares for them such security in holiness that they think they will persist immovable as regards lust more when joined than when separated; leading them on in all tranquillity, he disturbs them with no storms or waves, and, as if in the middle of the sea, he induces the less cautious to slacken the sails and not look for the rudder, so that he may drown them, shipwrecked and tossed by a sudden storm, in an unexpected upheaval. He first displays this mildness so as to entice two ships to come together, and when he has made them joined, he can dash them against each other with sudden whirlwinds and break them; and he uses these blandishments, withdrawing all his darts, restraining adversity, suggesting prosperity, and he hides the slumbering fire without any flames until, joining two torches, he sets both alight at once; and he refrains from setting the weapons of his savagery so long, until, like a skilled hunter, he binds what he is going to kill in the bonds of his snare. But when he has bound them fast with an unbreakable chain, like a gladiator-trainer he at once compels two gladiators to arm against each other, and then, goading their limbs, at once fits the swords, at once kindles the madness, and, driving them into wounding embraces, kills both at once with one blow. Thus he unfolds what he seems to have offered before; thus out of simple charity he forges an unlawful love; thus through holiness he brings in destruction; while he is content to yield, so he prevails to seize more strongly; and while, submissive, he allows himself to appear defeated, so he boasts of defeating more fully. The apostle Paul understands his cunning thus, saying: "For we are not ignorant," he says, "of his wiles." Badly, then, are they at peace in this partnership who are led on to war by the devil making peace, and they do not make good progress in holiness for whom progress itself is suborned to their harm by the enemy's artifice; nor do they strive with a straight course to climb the ladder of continence whom the adversary labours to draw out to the summit so as to hurl them from on high. But those must be dashed down in falling plunges who have kept to a slippery way, of which Solomon proclaims thus, saying: "There is [a way] which seems right among men, but its end comes into the depth of the underworld."

But they say: "If clerics are censured for this association, many saints too must be censured along with us: whether Elijah, who stayed with a widow; or the apostles, who took women about with them as companions, as John, who took the Lord's mother to himself at the Lord's own charge; or the Lord himself, to whom certain devout women provided food from their own means, whom Martha also served at table, and who spoke alone, sitting at the well, with a foreign woman of Samaria, or whose feet, as he reclined, a woman washed with tears and wiped with her hair." Clever arguers and deceitful lawyers, who, while they wish to act collusively, twist the disputes and pleadings of cases and even the laws themselves; and when they do not wish to be restrained by the applicable commands of the laws, they throw up, to make fools of the judges, unsuitable examples as if they were parallel inferences from the law. They are exposed through Solomon by the shrewdness of the law itself: "A sinful man," he says, "avoids reproof and finds a comparison to suit his will." Such men, therefore, must first be refuted not by discourse but by reproof, so that they are not instructed by explained discourses before they have lost what they found as a comfort for their defence; as Solomon teaches us against men of this kind, saying: "Do not answer a fool," he says, "according to his folly, lest you become like him; but answer a fool against his folly, so that he may not seem to himself to be wise."

Great men indeed, who compare themselves to the saints, and outstanding is our way of life, which is to be thought equal to the prophets or apostles! As an occasion for our self-indulgence we wish to imitate the saints perversely, and among their other acts we do not wish to follow the footsteps of the just. In some things we excuse ourselves as too weak to imitate the deeds of our elders, and in others we declare ourselves equal to our elders: although Elijah himself, placed in distress, confesses before God that he is unequal to his fathers: "Am I," he says, "better than my fathers?" Elijah is driven in his weakness to cry this out about his predecessors: and do we not hesitate to make our virtue equal to Elijah, or to the prophets and apostles and the Lord? I see clearly that avarice is trampled among us just as the apostles gave up all their own possessions. I see that gluttony and drunkenness are as absent from our banquets as the apostles, having nothing, were often forced to go hungry. I recognise that fasts, thirst, hunger, nakedness for the sake of urgency in teaching alone flourish everywhere among us in the way we read they triumphed in the apostles. And it is proved that among us the same exercises of virtue are fervent at which all vices trembled before the apostles. Clearly we practise the Lord's forty-day fast, and the prayers and vigils with which he broke even the silence of the night in solitary places. Do we engage in similar contests against the wrestlings of vices, and do we so act with rigour, authority, vigils, sufferings, labour, hardship, affliction, abstinence, by which sins are trampled, that no one suspects anything evil of us? Through these the apostle Paul boasts that his conscience was made known to all. "In all things," he says, "commending ourselves as ministers of God, in much endurance, in pressures, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in blows, in custodies, in prisons, in riots, in invocations, in labours, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in goodness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of justice on the right and on the left." For these imitations we are weak, but for taking women about we claim for ourselves the possibility of comparable imitation. But even if someone had boasted that he fulfilled all their deeds, still no one's persuasion could incline me to believe that there are now other apostles, against the declaration of the apostle Paul: "Are all," he says, "apostles? Are all prophets?" If Christ, who says, "The Father is greater than I," did not dare to compare himself to God, or if the apostles did not dare to make themselves equal to Christ, [how] should like strength today make us equal to the apostles? Wretched humanity, do you not fear to be struck by lightning in this equality, you who do not hesitate to borrow examples for your sins, as if similar, from the Son of God or from the sons of thunder? Since it would be the elated boasting of pride for anyone to wish to be enrolled as comparable even to the least of the church, since Paul warns and says: "Each esteeming the other superior to himself." And lower down he added, saying: "Have this mind about yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant."

Certainly we must think less of our own strength, and our weakness is not to be compared with the fortitude of the saints, as the apostle Paul sets before us instruction from himself and says: "For we do not dare," he says, "to compare or match ourselves with some who commend themselves; but we ourselves, commending ourselves to ourselves among ourselves, do not boast beyond measure but according to the measure of glory which God has measured out to us." But if we consider what he himself said again, "I laboured more than all of them," nothing better, nothing more fitting is set before me by which to win than that I myself should argue against them from the very man on whom they argue against me. Certainly he laboured more than all, and yet he trembled to imitate his colleagues in taking women about, lest he expose himself uncertainly to carnal temptation. Hence he himself gave the reason, saying: "I," he says, "so run, not as uncertainly; so I fight, not as beating the air; but I afflict my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, preaching to others, I myself be found reprobate." Compare yourself, then, to him, you who boast yourself an apostle, and learn from him what to fear, who cries out and says: "I beg you, be imitators of me." So he did not wish to have confidence about taking women about, he who was not unaware how much some virtues differ from other virtues, and had pointed out, drawing a likeness to the church's gifts, that the brightness of the sun is one thing and of the moon another, and of the stars another. But we, on the contrary, flatter ourselves on our equality with the apostles, not attending at all to what the apostles and all the saints did by unconquered virtue, and we seek to break through a difficult road when a smoother one through easy places is set before us, against Solomon, who says: "Do not trust yourself," he says, "to a toilsome road, lest you set a stumbling block for your soul." Nor does anyone consider that one man walks safely on slippery ground and another who is unequal to it slips; one climbs mountains at a run over crags and another, if he strains himself, falls; it falls to one to bring ships happily through storms, and such good fortune cannot befall another; as the apostle Paul decides, saying: "Each," he says, "has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that."

But those who prejudge against me from the example of the saints, why will they not consider another example that they should fear? And he who strives to be made equal to the apostles, why does he not rather set before himself, to frighten himself, the adulterous elders in Daniel? I do not put this forward in order to contradict, as it were, imitators of the apostles, but to confound those who make themselves equal to the saints. Nor do I deny that those whom we have all received as teachers are to be followed; but I contend against those who, wishing to distort the histories of good men to their own evil ends, think the law supports them, as all do who hasten to perish, so that under the pretext of the saints they wish their disgraces to be hidden, so that under imitation of the elders they may commit every contrary thing: whom the apostle Paul exposes and makes public, saying: "But what I do, I will also do, to cut off the occasion of those who want an occasion, so that in what they boast of they may be found such as we are. For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ." They add this to heap up the heap of their perdition, that they defame the good whose example they use for evil; for whom it would be useful and wholesome enough if they believed rather that they had not understood the reason of some history than to think there was anything dishonourable in the law. The apostle Paul confounds and rebukes them, saying: "Understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm." And again: "If anyone thinks he knows something, he has not yet known as he ought to know." Void, therefore, are the prejudgements of the insolent, whom the wandering wits of their perversity lead astray, and who seek histories suited to their own views to expound; who, acting badly, borrow the patronage of the law. But to those who act well, all things that are written are good, who receive well what is well said, as the apostle Paul assures: "We know," he says, "that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully."

We have prevailed by confounding our opponents. Next we turn to instruct further the same men we have defeated, so that we neither allow the saints to remain under accusation nor be reckoned ignorant in giving an account, so that, publicly defeated, they may do penance; or, if they will not, we have discharged what belongs to our diligence, so that as we have satisfied the saying of Solomon mentioned above, so we may satisfy also the apostle Paul when he preaches: "The servant of the Lord," he says, "must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, teachable, patient, rebuking with all modesty those who resist, in case God may perhaps give them repentance to know the truth, and they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will."

Everything that was done by our authorities was done for a reason, so that an authority fortified on every side might be handed down to us who came after, against transgressors. To forestall the heresy which we censured above, the Lord relaxed a little on taking women along, whether by himself or through his servants, so that the Lord's handiwork might not be wholly condemned through excessive rigour. The Lord foresaw the heretics who abolish marriage and strive to separate, against the first principle of nature and against the gospel, those whom the Lord has joined. Even then an authority was being prepared to forbid them, so that married women should not be prevented from approaching Christ, whom they served in [his] presence. But even this permission was not arranged without restraint, for what it did, it did not for itself but for others. For if the Lord spoke with the Samaritan woman, he taught her for an hour and withdrew, and he made no defence for prolonging excesses. For an hour he also allowed Martha to serve. But what else was it for the Lord than to serve the meals of the heavenly kingdom? Were there not feasts under the Lord? Or in his majesty was there any other drink or food than the teaching alone which fed them? As the Lord himself testifies, saying: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me." So a company of women escorted the apostles, not that they might ruin them but that they might learn reverence, and they followed in order to render the service of kindness, as is recorded in the gospel of the Lord and of them alike: "And it came to pass," it says, "after these things that he too journeyed through cities and villages, preaching the kingdom of God, and the twelve with him, and women who had been cured of unclean spirits and infirmities, Mary who is called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, who also ministered to him from their means."

Did they cling as single men to single women, or persist in an undisciplined cohabitation, living in an enticing companionship, where almost the whole church could see, so that they followed not for shameless feasting but to learn the pursuits of a good way of life? So far is anything described there that could be likened to our feasts that no laughter, no joking, is said to have been present. Nor is a choir of virgins singing psalms said to have soothed [their] ears with poisonous songs, as is customary among some even now. And to prove briefly from the apostles how much loose familiarity could displease them: they were driven to doubt even about the Lord himself speaking with a woman, had not their proven knowledge of his majesty restrained them. As the evangelist relates, saying: "Meanwhile," he says, "his disciples came and marvelled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said to him: 'What do you seek, or why do you speak with her?'" And why should I speak of the approach of the woman who threw herself at the Lord's feet, whose grief and lamentation the shameless do not blush to demand in defence of their own wantonness? Their own blindness carries them so far that they do not dare even to struggle against similar cases, about which Solomon says: "Their malice has blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God." John, it seems, took in the Lord's mother. But a mother whose character the name of mother points to. Yet I cannot admit other mothers of Christ as well, nor is she who bore [his] majesty to be made equal to all women. Elijah too was ordered by the Lord to leave the wilderness and enter a widow's dwelling. At the Lord's command he toiled to stay in a house, he for whom the wilderness served as a palace for rest: the Lord offered him an occasion for doing great works, so that in a time of famine he himself might rather supply sufficient food to the widow and to her orphans, he who, afflicted everywhere by fasting, had endured want; and he who had been sent and had come to be fed, instead feeding [them], bestowing [aid] on the wretched, caused the wretchedness of poverty to be shut out. And this cannot favour anyone's laxity, since there was no opportunity for a stumbling block, where in passing he had, what is worse, a needy lodging which any guest would flee. But he fulfilled [his task] among those with whom he lodged and went back; and even if he had stayed, he could not have been suspected. What sort of attachment of shared life was there, where there was no food? And what sort of entry to the widow did Elijah have, to whom famine gave hospitality? Whoever you are who wish to be called a disciple of Elijah on the ground of his staying with the widow, first endure the afflictions of the wilderness and the end of forty days fasting, and either you will not seek a woman or there will be no one to stay with a woman; and yet, if you are able, keep [it] for yourself. But to us the angel and the Lord Christ point to no one other than John alone as [coming] in the spirit and power of Elijah.

Oh, shame! We are forced to grieve at what we teach, we who have come to this, that we argue about the dread virtues of the saints in comparison with loose men. Spare [us] now, spare [us], insolence. The saints never agree with you, who conducted their dealings with women in a religious, modest, venerable, chaste and decent way. Or if you still strive to search out winding quibbles by means of the saints, we nevertheless know that the friends of God are to be mentioned only for veneration, as David taught, saying: "But to me your friends are greatly honoured, O God." Let the robbers of modesty and kidnappers of chastity go now and set out the troubles of their complaints to their little women. Among our saints they have no refuge at all, and the church is forbidden by the authority of the apostle Paul to mix with them. "And these," he says, "avoid: for of these are those who creep into houses and lead captive little women laden with sins, who are led by various desires."

After this edict, would that they might trust that the examples of angels help them. They can no longer sway us, who know that angels too fell with women. From them indeed they borrow a fitting patronage; but we heed no angel against the apostle Paul. "But even if we," he says, "or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be anathema." Utterly mad are they, and hot with the fire of women, as many as do not yield to this prohibition, and, gaping after obscenities, they would rather die than consent to be torn from women's sides by any separation, so that, to fill up the filth of their greed, they may not be without a woman's pleasure even for a moment of time; and this is the fruit they have in women, that with their attention always fixed on them they sate the desires of their eyes, lest even a single moment pass in which they lacked what they crave. So integrity dies among them, where every cohabitation, whether by living together or by dwelling together, is defiled by corrupt affections. Saint Peter had marked them out, saying: "Revelling in their feasts, having eyes full of adulteries and ceaseless sins, enticing weak souls." Solomon too denounces them: "An abomination," he says, "before the Lord is he who fixes his eye." Job plainly testifies that he keeps a pure eye, saying: "And if my heart has consented to my eyes." Truly indeed that man can be held not guilty through his eyes, in whom, against his will, a sudden meeting with a woman has stirred a stumbling block, since the mind at once drives out what it did not want. But he does not deserve to escape the disturbance of his sight who keeps the material of a stumbling block at home, who wants to enjoy the affections of his attention, who craves to have what thrusts offence upon the eyes, whose insatiable greed amid continual stumbling blocks can in no way at all be restrained; as Solomon confirms, saying: "Hell and destruction are not satisfied; likewise the eyes of men are insatiable." And in another place: "The eye is not satisfied with seeing." And again: "What has been created more wicked than the eye?"

Not pricked by this rebuke, they despise the divine prohibitions with the obstinacy of an unspeakable familiarity, and moreover they still plead charity, when, according to the word of Isaiah, they swallow bitterness for sweetness and cover naked foulness with the veil of a good name, and among them true love is violated under false love. But charity cries out and appeals: "I did not join such people; let that other go who fabricates me by pretence. I never oppose God's commandments, I never favour the loose, I do not wish holiness to be blamed through me. A hostile brotherhood makes false charges against me; I too have met with dangers among false brothers. Help, my herald, help, apostle Paul, give my testimony, lest what you proclaim of me be perverted: 'Now the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned.'" Will that be reckoned love, through which holiness is assailed with the injury of accusations? Or is their brotherhood to be judged sincere, through whom the daughters of mother church are led into guilt? If such is marked as Christian charity, then without doubt hatreds are better, which, while they separate, stain no one. But this parricidal love has been accustomed to unite persecuting brothers, who gladly allow the daughters of the church to be defamed as fornicators on account of their companionship, against the charity which the apostle Paul taught, saying: "Love of neighbour works no evil." A splendid proof of charity, which not only harms the neighbour by a noxious brotherhood but also does not wish to be subject to the prescriptions of the apostolic command. Let the champions of love of this kind be put to shame; they are judged by those who for the common good abandon even the love of kin.

Almost the whole human race is joined together throughout the world, and everywhere natural kinship is divided by its members going abroad from one another. Parents can, children can, brothers can, and, what is more, spouses themselves can break the bonds of nature granted to them by God; and are clerics unable to refuse a charity enslaved to the ties of women, which God does not grant and even forbids? The closeness of their nearest, always to be longed for, is given up by kinsfolk, and do clerics resist going away from women who are strangers to them? They ought to have done it even if the Lord had commanded something peculiar or unaccustomed, since for accomplishing impossible things they have the Holy Spirit, which worldly men do not have. Hence the apostle John admonishes thus, saying: "Little children, overcome them, for greater is he who is in you than [he who is] in this world." But now what is possible even for the gentiles, not to say for Christians, is looked on as a light matter and among clerics is emptied of any effect, so that it is not enough for them to despise the commandments of God unless they have a further disgrace: they do not even follow, not to say surpass, the custom of all the nations. These the Lord reproaches through Ezekiel and says: "You have not walked in my statutes and have not done my ordinances, and you have not even done according to the ordinances of the nations that are round about you." This love signifies something shameful, when it is thought to be wrested from them against nature.

I still have something to wonder at: when I see that many Christians, husbands and wives alike, resolving on continence, prefer to choose separate dwellings, so that by an agreed withdrawal they may keep the consent of their shared vows without the provocation of each other's presence, can our eunuchs not bear to sleep without a woman's company? Among those, conjugal love is outweighed by love of continence, and among the eunuchs cohabitation with a woman can never produce weariness. Let the charity of the eunuchs speak now, let it speak, lest perhaps conjugal charity sins rather in this withdrawal, so that the counsel of the apostle Paul might seem to have suggested divorce to spouses: "The time," he says, "that remains is short. It remains that those who have wives be as though they had none." What perversity of love is aimed at, that those who have [wives] strive to be as though they had none, and those who have none boast of being as though they had [them]. Of these the apostle himself says: "Their glory is in their shame."

"It is love," they say. O love that envies itself! O charity that longs to be praised with reproach! A great marvel, that the charity of virgins makes virgins believed to be like spouses, and the charity of spouses makes spouses reckoned like virgins. Behold true love, which divides in marriage in order to join in chastity. Behold holy love, which leads married people to separation for their common praise. These assuredly love each other inseparably, who part from each other in order to win triumphs for themselves: from them neither crime nor nature nor law nor the Lord nor the apostle forbade or took away the right of a single life together, but charity persuaded them to live apart, their unanimity set at a distance, in order to keep equal vows. But let those see whose charity it is that they know, who yield neither to crime nor to nature nor to law nor to the Lord nor to the apostle nor to marriage itself; whom a shameful virginity condemns as much as a castrated marriage glorifies those others. Let it be enough for their disgraceful punishment that eunuchs are judged by married people. For their rebuke the sons of Israel too must not be passed over in silence, who in [the book of] Ezra did not hesitate to drive out the wives and children they had taken against divine law, nor tried to excuse themselves by appeal to the Lord's charity. Let me speak the truth, if I am permitted. Those who now cling [to them] rather than send away women who are not their own, what would they do if they were ordered to cast off children and wives? Or when will they be able to renounce kinsfolk for Christ, who put little women not their own before the precepts of Christ? I say they would more easily deny their own parents for the sake of these same little women than be able to leave the little women themselves for the sake of Christ, despising what the Lord himself testified in the gospel, saying: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father or mother or wife and children and brothers and sisters and his own soul, he cannot be my disciple."

If those who hesitate to cast off their parents are unworthy of Christ, what do they promise themselves whom no affection for parents, [but something else], shows to be despisers of Christ? And so they are emptied [of worth] by the merits of those whom they see, out of regard for Christ, making no exception of any kinsfolk. No less, but even worse, do those put them to shame who, fearing to wrestle not only with another's flesh but even with their own, cut themselves off by amputating their genitals. Concerning these I suspend for now my verdict on examination, leaving it to be set out in another discussion. But to the shame of the eunuchs I do not hesitate to declare them better, who do not spare even themselves, not to say dare to hold out temptations to women. Let the spiritual eunuchs answer: what madness is there in the love of women, or what mystery in sharing a dwelling with a woman, that they indulge others' members to their own ruin, when those others cut off even their own without hesitation? These cast away limbs firmly set in themselves, and those glue themselves to hostile limbs. These do not hesitate to fight for spiritual integrity with the torment of a body no longer whole, and those, without torment, refuse to be whole without the half that is women. But no comparison of our men should be made against those, lest they who are condemned by every Christian judgment take comfort. There are others too, worse, to be mentioned, so that the punishment may be greater to be condemned by the condemned. Let them consider the Jews, who to this day at the command of the law cut off part of their flesh by the torment of circumcision, and let them know what they deserve who, though the gospel commands it, neglect to do the Lord's will by being circumcised from the presence of women, not understanding that the Lord himself said: "Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." I think even the idolaters may taunt us reproachfully with their Galli, who willingly torture themselves by cutting themselves, so long as, at the loss of their condition, they obey the pretences of idols. But our clerics, for the gain rather of their own body, are willing to bear the loss of women living with them, whom they ought to tear away even from their own substance if it had happened that they were born with them, lest compared with idolaters and sacrilegious men they should blush. Of such the Lord too convicts the despisers, saying: "The sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light." Therefore the profane devotion of such people is to be preferred to our clerics, since to them base priesthoods are lovable at the cost of such great ruin. But clerics, for the dignity of the heavenly priesthood, shed no blood, endure no iron, there is no wound, there is no torture; but the mere sight of a woman burns them against the Lord. So they rush upon women, so they love women, that they do not expect that the pure mysteries of their love can ever be made manifest, as they have been shamefully published and uncovered through men like them, whom the apostle Paul had already then foreseen, saying: "The sins of some men are manifest, going before to judgment, but some they also follow after. Likewise also good deeds are manifest, and whatever are otherwise cannot be hidden."

But they in turn also say: "Some of those who despised us, likewise having women in their houses, attained martyrdom, so that among them an innocent conscience was proved." I do not want anyone to bring a case before me on the matter of martyrdom, since very often adulterers and murderers and drunkards and those guilty of all crimes, having found an occasion for combat and turned [to God], have deserved to attain the pardon of martyrdom. For martyrdom is called both a crown and a baptism for this reason, that it baptises and crowns alike. Come now, if it was granted to some to earn martyrdom while their company with women was inviolate, yet martyrdom itself was not without pardon even for those whom the guilt of forbidden cohabitation did not absolve; nor could it prove innocent in that very innocence those for whom it is seen to have pardoned contempt of the law and the foulness of an illicit way of life and, what is graver than all, a crime against the church. For innocence is harmful which damages the reputation of the bride of Christ. And since Christ, the innocent lamb, or rather, more truly, heavenly innocence itself, spent his whole self for the church, to render her untouched without any spot or wrinkle, what kind of cleric is he to whom the bride of Christ is entrusted, that he allows the whole church to be blamed for the love of one woman? I would dare to say: the Son was sent by God the Father from the bosom of the Father and endured being absent from the kingdom in order to make the church innocent, and a cleric cannot leave a woman's side lest he make Christ's church infamous?

But they say: "In martyrdom we are forgiven, just as it was granted to our forebears." Then let us all trust in this too concerning all sins, so that we who labour to act well may wander among luxuries and run about the paths of sins, let go the reins and slacken the bridles. Let us go wherever the world carries us off and wherever the devil invites us; let us freely fornicate, envy, rob, cheat, commit all evils without care: martyrdom will come to our aid and we shall escape. For so the apostle Paul promises: "Let us do evil that good may come": "their condemnation is just." Let those place their hope in this martyrdom whom astrologers have taught to have foreknowledge of tomorrow, and let those await these crowns who, above the angels and Christ, have learned through astrologers to know the times which the Father has set in his own power, so that they may at least then remember that they ought to have acted well before the time of martyrdom, when they perceive the day of the Lord [coming] like a thief. But let us believe that martyrdom is hanging over them any moment now. Meanwhile, before they become martyrs, they are subject to the laws, so as to be brought to judgment, unless they are disarmed of their arms. It is wicked audacity in them to set the persons of their forebears against the authority of the Lord: the Lord himself has taken away from them the voice of this objection. "Do not walk," he says, "in the statutes of your fathers and do not keep their ordinances, and do not mingle in their pursuits and do not be defiled. I am the Lord your God. Walk in my precepts and keep my ordinances."

Let those now know that the defence of their forebears has been taken from them, who, running back and forth, look for hiding-places in objections so that they may never be without women. And since they are left on every side without any support for their defence, at the last, with all arguments exhausted, they suppose that a saying of the apostle Paul helps them, and they say: "Who are you to judge another's servant?" The apostle Paul indeed recognises the words of his own ruling that they bring forward, but he does not know the rule-makers and those who bring it forward. For he gave that defence to those who attack no part of the law, and he granted that protection to those who do something by their own free choice and obstruct nothing of church law. He is dealing with the right of eating and not eating, confirming each person's free choice. In like matters he ordered that no one be judged, since divine authority, granting these to the will of individuals, mercifully allowed either course, of doing and of not doing. But he subjected to the church's tribunals those whom no impunity excused as transgressors against the established order, so that those who everywhere bring out "Who are you to judge another's servant?" against us like a counter-plea may recognise the rebuttal, reasoned and certain at once, which we have received from the same apostle Paul. "We command you, brothers," he says, "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to separate yourselves from brothers who walk disorderly and not according to the tradition which you received from us."

We have escaped, I think, such great knots of questions, with which the embraces of women have bound eunuchs who are lovers, who are driven to alter the decrees of the law by perverse interpretations, and who prefer to be heard putting forward empty and fabulous inventions rather than to hear for themselves what is true. Of them the apostle Paul gives warning, saying: "They will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth and will be turned to fables." Whatever else they still wish to search out so as to resist the truth on behalf of women, they do not have the victory, among whom, against Esdras, woman rather than truth has won. But you, dearest sons, I address not only with persuasion but also with authority. Despise such raving, people whose questions you know the apostle Paul everywhere condemned, as he wrote to the Romans, saying: "I ask you, brothers, to watch carefully those who either say or do things causing dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and turn away from them." So too he charges Timothy: "Do not," he says, "contend about words, for it is of no use, except to the subversion of the hearers. Take care to show yourself approved to God, a workman beyond reproach, rightly handling the word of truth. But avoid foolish and empty talk, for it advances greatly towards impiety, and their speech creeps like a cancer."
