And to show what teaching is fitting for clerics to be appointed to empty out such questions, he also instructs Titus thus, saying: "But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine: that the elders be sober, prudent, sound in faith, in charity, in sincere patience." Therefore let your obedience accept plain teachings, and avoid the shifty deceit of objections. Clear a clean path for your steps and do not tread upon thorns and thistles, lest because of the thorn-bushes the good seed cannot bring you the fruits of holiness. Hence the prophet Jeremiah exhorts and teaches thus, saying: "Do not," he says, "sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to your God, circumcise the foreskin of your heart." So everything that is accustomed to prick and tear must be cut out of your field, lest the mind of the farmer be entangled in malignant briars on his own property. And we must cut off everything that the furnace of seething flesh, bubbling with the sulphurous flames of fiery kindling, boils up, lest even a slight spark kept alive should blow up greater fires. Solomon makes this plain, saying: "From one spark the fire grows." Turn away impure occasions, by which the inner parts of the breast are pierced, so that a clear transparency may be honoured in you. Be content rather to endure a laborious solitude for the sake of keeping your modesty than to arrive at disgrace without labour.

Consider what it is to preside over a holy people, and reflect what kind of thing it is to attend upon the divine sacraments. Those who live by the altars must please the altars, and the care for sincerity befitting consecrated men must be such as the sacred things themselves to which they render the duties of service, lest towards the Lord they themselves offend against what they handle, or towards the people they begin to obstruct what they preach. For this reason the apostle Paul testifies thus and says: "And we endure all things," he says, "lest we give any hindrance to the gospel of Christ." And again: "Giving no offence to anyone, so that our ministry may not be reproached." By this instruction, then, you must labour as much as possible in those matters for which, to show seriousness of life, solitude rather than pairing is the true witness. See how many evils the way of life of this pairing acquires: it sows nothing but corruption, it sprouts vices, conceives desire, gives birth to disgrace, stirs up rage, extends frenzy, feeds lewdness, nourishes wantonness, exalts falls, builds ruins; it raises banks, constructs precipices, sails through dangers, sets its sails for shipwrecks, rejoices in perdition, cherishes destruction, purchases confusion, treasures up reproach, heaps up charges, inflames accusations, and, gathering into one bundle in crowds numerous snares of entrapment, through endless disgraces it brings manifold deaths upon the ruined to their destruction.

So many and such great slaughters of calamity and of the worst way of life no one lays low, no one tramples, no one puts to death, except solitary chastity alone, which is the unconquered bulwark of holiness and the strong storming of infamy, the firmness of strength and the weakening of wanton lewdness, the defence of uprightness and the destruction of wickedness, the victory of the soul and the plunder of the body, the abundance of glories and the captivity of crimes, the bridesmaid of holiness and the divorce of baseness, the proof of sincerity and the abolition of stumbling blocks, the exercise of continence and the complete emptying of luxury, the secure peace of the virtues and the quiet ending of wars, the summit of purity and the prison of lust, the harbour of honour and the place of shipwreck for disgrace, the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness, the breastplate of modesty and the despoiling of shamefulness, the ruin of corruption, the wall of strictness and the destruction of promiscuity, the sword of severity, the triumpher over and slayer of laxity, the armour of strength and the disarming of dissipations, the dignity of integrity and the condemnation of fornication, the pinnacle of renown and the precipice of disgrace, the will for good works and the affliction of vices, the refreshment of chastity and the punishment of wantonness, the acquiring of triumphs and the loss of crimes, the rest of salvation and the exile of perdition, the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh, the state of angelic nature, the funeral of human substance. By its reins all obscenity is bridled, and by its fetters the heels of raging lust are held fast. On it, as on a rock, every surge of overflowing blood is broken, and in it the foaming madness of bodily swelling is calmed. While it withdraws from itself the supports of desire, it is known to carry its members as dead, of which the apostle Paul forewarns, saying: "Put to death, therefore, your members which are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire and avarice, which is the service of idols, on account of which the wrath of God comes."

From all these things human nature is castrated only by the shining knife of solitude, so that, with circumcision acting as betrother, it may bring unblemished eunuchs into the banquet of holiness. To it holiness has promised the nuptial seal of her ring in such a way that without it virginity is unsealed; content with itself alone, it tames desire and makes the mind chaste, subdues concupiscence, quenches the desires of burning, weakens the limbs, enslaves the body, and so crucifies the things of the flesh that both male and female appear to belie [their sex] in their way of life, since it cuts them off from the activity of either sex: or, making neither of the two, it glories in conferring a third form upon both, so that before the resurrection it is known to rehearse the image of the resurrection after the likeness of the angels. Promising this for the future, the Lord says: "Those who are held worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage, nor indeed will they die. For they are like the angels of God, because they are sons of the resurrection." This the holy solitude of merits demands, that before it is transfigured it is already seen transfigured into the appearance of angelic brightness; cutting all things away from itself, it plunders the struggles of desire. Solomon sets out its praises, saying: "It is better to be without children, with renown. For immortality is in its memory, since it is known both with God and with men. When it is present they imitate it, and they long for it when it has departed; and crowned for ever it triumphs, winning the battle of undefiled contests."

None is "without children, with renown" except solitude alone, which not only does its own conscience stain with no filth, but also no suspicions of pairing defame. For even if chastity, which is difficult, should keep a man and a woman alike in virginity, it does not have renown, which the shared life itself cannot but obscure with some darkness of disgraces. But solitude is so clear and open to all that it is shown to everyone pure and bright by the splendour of its whiteness. Hence the apostle teaches us thus, saying: "Walk as sons of light: for the fruit of light is in all goodness and justice and truth, proving what is well-pleasing to God." And again: "Do all things," he says, "without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be beyond reproach and simple, as spotless sons of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world." So solitude shines everywhere, so that all do not hesitate to vouch for it, and it so glorifies holiness in itself that it wrests praise for itself even from its enemies. This the apostle Paul especially enjoins concerning any overseer, saying: "He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil." Love this, then, hold to this, which alone can conquer women. While as yet no desire strikes the breast, and while simplicity still remains uncorrupted or at rest, run quickly to the secret protection of solitude, lest afterwards you be unable to escape.

The approach must be blocked in advance against all ambushes, so that the enemy does not creep up first and come upon the unprepared. It is a saving remedy to forestall rather than be forestalled, and it befits brave men to anticipate rather than be anticipated. Wherever there is foresight, all adversities are thwarted; but where foresight is neglected, all adversities rule. Before hunger comes we strive, before want comes we busy ourselves with labour. So in all things we leave no room for any calamities, while we exercise foresight for the times to come. How much more must the calamity of women be forestalled with every precaution, since the desire for them, once it is allowed to begin, never reaches an end at all? Solomon sets out its likeness, saying: "Hell, and the love of a woman, and the earth that is not filled with water, and fire, do not say: It is enough." So let each one who is secure because he is not yet tempted be afraid. Because nothing is said about him, let him take care that nothing is said. We are men; we carry our frailty in the flesh. So we ought now to surround and gird ourselves on every side with watchful alertness, so that there is no part that wavers. We do indeed receive a spiritual strength, by which the frailty of our substance is strengthened. But spiritual strength has been granted to us so that it may protect the prudent, not the reckless; so that it may fortify those who renounce the importunities of sins, not those who plunge themselves the more into importunate sins. The Spirit has been given to us as a guardian, but so that by standing by he may help those who turn away from adversities, not so that he may favour those who choose adversities; nor so that he may strengthen those who go willingly and headlong into what is hostile, but so that he may confirm those who strive to be separated from what is hostile. For whoever dares to exercise his virtue in ruinous attempts does not have the help of the Holy Spirit, who wills that no man be forced, of his own accord, to be brave for the sake of deceitful victories. Nor does he protect, but rather deserts, the one whom he knows to be rushing into dangers to seek triumphs through unlawful outcomes, as he himself said long ago through Solomon, saying: "He who loves danger will perish in it."

So the power of the Holy Spirit is supplied in his own order, not at our discretion, and battles prosper according to his ordinance. No army has ever fallen unless it was thrown headlong, eager to act bravely and breaking through the dispositions of its general or commander. Much more does he spend a strength doomed to perish who presumes to triumph without the arms of the teaching of the Spirit, his master, since it says: "Woe to those who do anything through their own presumption, not through God."

If, then, there is in you any confidence in spiritual strength, let it remember what befits spiritual men; and if you believe that you serve as soldiers in a spiritual way, recognise that what we teach is not carnal, as the apostle Paul speaks, saying: "If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge what I write to you." There is no reason for you to flatter yourselves with this deceptive persuasion, that because you are spiritual you may wish to move about among the weapons of the wicked, nor [to think] that you are not liable [to danger] because of the dignity of the clergy; for greater conflicts are accustomed to come upon greater men. The rich are envied more bitterly than the poor, and the savage assault of robbers troubles not the needy but the wealthy. Generals and princes are attacked by enemies in battle more than soldiers, and whatever summits are higher are battered more violently by winds and whirlwinds. Therefore, the more each one is capable beyond others, the more and more let him know that he must fear lest he be diminished in anything; on which account Solomon admonishes thus, saying: "He who glories," he says, "in riches, let him fear poverty." I beg you, as much as I am able and beyond what I am able, let this be the endeavour of all clerics: that they keep to the retreat of an unimpeachable solitude, so that neither they through women nor women through them are provoked to shameful mockeries. If anyone has a mother or daughter or sister or wife or kinswoman, let him have her in such a way that no maidservant is present and no outside woman enters, lest he seem to keep his relatives with him for this purpose, that on their account he may freely bring other women in to himself. But if those who are his relatives cannot be without the service of maids or without the comfort of female friends, it is better that they move to another dwelling than that, because of them, persons who are a danger be kept. For it is humane that neither the cleric deprive them of women they need, nor they defile the cleric through troublesome women. They can be assigned to holy women with whom to live, provided that no woman stays with the cleric. No woman, not even a despised one or an old one, who is not a relative, is to be taken in specially for domestic service; for sin is committed more quickly where sin can be safe from suspicion, especially since for desire no ugliness, no contemptibility is repellent or worthless, for the devil, painting it over, makes beautiful whatever is foul or hideous.

But if anyone, compelled by a journey, lodges with brothers or with strangers where women are present, let him restrain himself entirely, so that he is not corrupted by any susceptibility. Withdrawn and apart, let him give his time to God and to himself, lest he be captured indoors by the devil, and he who could not be captured outside should fall among his own people, he who escaped the enemy. Let him come into their presence for a time for salutary reasons, and hasten quickly to leave their sight again. Everywhere presence with women is to be tasted, not prolonged; rather, access to women is to be granted in passing, as it were in a fugitive manner. For the beginnings of wantonness are always brought out into the open, and to make a habit of frequent going among women is a rehearsal of perdition. On this matter Solomon has imposed a limit on us, saying: "Do not be constantly in the midst of women." So walk, then, so act, that the senate of the Church may always stand spotless in its clerics. Let severity towards women flourish in us, let authority prevail, let vigour be kept, let gravity be revered.

To gather everything once and for all into a conclusion, we read back to you a summary which the apostle Paul conveys, reducing it to a concise fullness: "For the rest," he says, "brothers, whatever things are true, whatever are chaste, whatever are just, whatever are holy, whatever are lovable, whatever are of good report, if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think on these things, which you have received and learned and heard and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace and love will be with you." Amen.
